name: THE ONE YAM BAND BURGER - (Comes with yams)

recipe.history:
The yam — true yam, Dioscorea species — is one of the oldest cultivated crops on earth, with roots (literal and figurative) stretching back over ten thousand years to West and Central Africa. Unlike the orange-fleshed sweet potato that most Americans casually call a yam, true yams are starchy, off-white or purple-fleshed tubers that can grow to extraordinary sizes, some varieties topping a hundred pounds. In West African culinary traditions, yams hold a sacred cultural status: the Igbo of Nigeria celebrate the New Yam Festival, or Iri Ji, as a harvest ceremony of profound communal and spiritual significance. Yams were pounded into fufu, roasted over open fires, fried into crispy chips, and stewed into soups that fed entire villages. When enslaved Africans were brought to the Americas during the transatlantic slave trade, they carried with them not only their labor but their food memory — and the yam traveled with them, renamed, misidentified, and conflated with the sweet potato, yet never fully forgotten.

The confusion between yams and sweet potatoes in American cuisine is not merely linguistic — it is a story of cultural displacement and culinary adaptation. Sweet potatoes (Ipomoea batatas), native to Central and South America, were already growing in the American South when African enslaved people arrived, and their soft, orange flesh reminded those people enough of the yams from home that the name stuck colloquially. Southern cooks — both Black and white — developed the sweet potato into a cornerstone of regional cuisine: candied yams with brown sugar and marshmallows, sweet potato pie, sweet potato biscuits, and eventually sweet potato fries. The leap from side dish to burger topping followed the broader American culinary revolution of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, when chefs began raiding the pantry of soul food and Southern cooking for ingredients that could add sweetness, earthiness, and textural contrast to the savory umami bomb of a well-made beef burger. Roasted or fried yam slices, caramelized and slightly crisp at the edges, proved to be a natural companion to a medium-rare patty — the sweetness cutting through the fat, the starch anchoring the whole structure.

I first encountered this combination on a cold Tuesday in November, the kind of day when the sky sits low and gray and the whole world smells like wet leaves and radiator heat. I was eating alone at a small counter-service place near the waterfront, the sort of restaurant with mismatched chairs and a chalkboard menu that changes every week. The burger arrived without ceremony: a slightly asymmetrical brioche bun, a patty that was clearly still pink inside (I could tell by the way it yielded when I pressed it gently with one finger), and two thick coins of roasted yam draped over the top with a smear of something smoky and orange. The first bite was revelatory in the quiet way that certain foods are — not a thunderclap but a long, warm resonance, the way a familiar song sounds when you hear it in an unexpected place. The sweetness of the yam against the iron-rich, mineral depth of the beef made something that was greater than the sum of its parts. I sat there longer than I needed to, not because the restaurant was particularly comfortable, but because I didn't want the feeling to end. That is what a great burger does. It holds you still for a moment in a world that rarely stops moving.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef burger patty, and that temperature is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a matter of personal preference — it is a matter of physics, chemistry, and respect for the animal and the craft. At medium rare, the muscle fibers have contracted just enough to firm the patty into a cohesive structure while retaining the majority of their intracellular moisture. The fat within the grind has begun to render and redistribute, basting the meat from the inside. The Maillard reaction on the exterior crust is complete — brown, complex, faintly bitter in the best possible way — while the interior remains a deep rose, almost magenta at the very center, yielding to the tooth with a gentle resistance that communicates life and care. Cook a patty to well done and you have committed a culinary irreversibility: the proteins have seized, the moisture has fled, the fat has burned off, and what remains is a disk of compacted protein that no amount of sauce or topping can fully redeem. The One Yam Band Burger, with its sweet and earthy yam topping, deserves a patty that can hold its own — and only a medium-rare patty has the juice, the funk, and the presence to stand beside something so boldly flavored. Cook it right. There are no exceptions.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
400g freshly ground beef chuck (80/20 lean-to-fat ratio)
100g freshly ground beef brisket (for additional fat and flavor)
2 medium yams or garnet sweet potatoes (about 500g total), peeled
2 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, minced
4 slices aged white cheddar or gouda cheese
Neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola), for the griddle or cast iron
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — START 4 HOURS AHEAD: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to combine. Add the 2 eggs and warmed milk. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.
2. Increase mixer speed to medium and knead the dough for 5 minutes until it begins to come together and pull away from the sides of the bowl.

3. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is fully incorporated before adding the next. This process will take 8 to 10 minutes. The dough will look greasy and separated at first — keep going. It will eventually become smooth, glossy, and elastic.

4. Continue kneading on medium speed for another 5 minutes until the dough passes the windowpane test: stretch a small piece between your fingers and it should stretch thin enough to see light through without tearing.

5. Shape the dough into a ball, place it in a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours (or overnight). Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the dough easier to handle.

6. Remove dough from refrigerator and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 130g each). Shape each portion into a tight ball by pulling the sides under and pinching at the bottom. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced at least 3 inches apart. Flatten each ball gently with your palm to about 1 inch thickness.
7. Cover loosely with a clean kitchen towel and let proof at room temperature until doubled and puffy, 60 to 90 minutes.
8. Preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make the egg wash. Brush each bun gently with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.

9. Bake for 14 to 16 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through, until the buns are deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing. Do not rush this step — cutting a hot brioche bun will compress it.

10. MAKE THE SMOKY CHIPOTLE MAYO: In a small bowl, combine the mayonnaise, minced chipotle peppers, adobo sauce, lime juice, garlic powder, smoked paprika, and salt. Stir until fully combined. Taste and adjust heat with additional chipotle if desired. Cover and refrigerate until assembly.

11. CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: In a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet over medium-low heat, melt the butter with the olive oil. Add the sliced onions and salt. Stir to coat. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 35 to 45 minutes. The onions should slowly turn golden and jammy — do not rush this with high heat or they will burn rather than caramelize.

12. In the last 5 minutes of cooking, add the brown sugar and balsamic vinegar to the onions. Stir to combine and cook until the liquid is absorbed and the onions are deep amber and glossy. Remove from heat and set aside.

13. ROAST THE YAMS: Preheat oven to 425°F / 220°C. Slice the peeled yams into rounds approximately 1/2 inch thick. In a large bowl, whisk together the olive oil, melted butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, cumin, smoked paprika, cayenne, salt, and pepper. Add the yam slices and toss until every piece is evenly coated.

14. Spread the yam slices in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Do not overlap. Roast for 15 minutes, then flip each slice with a spatula and roast for another 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are caramelized and slightly crisp and the centers are fork-tender. Remove from oven and keep warm.

15. FORM THE PATTIES: Combine the ground chuck and ground brisket in a large bowl. Using your hands, gently mix until just combined — do not overwork the meat or the patties will be dense and tough. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 125g each).

16. Form each portion into a patty approximately 4 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb — this prevents the patty from doming as it cooks. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper. Refrigerate the formed patties for at least 15 minutes to help them hold their shape.

17. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place the patties dimple-side up in the pan — do not press them down. Cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms on the bottom.

18. Flip the patties once. Immediately add the butter, thyme sprigs, and smashed garlic to the pan. As the butter melts and foams, tilt the pan slightly and use a large spoon to baste the patties continuously with the herb butter for 1 to 2 minutes.

19. Begin checking internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer inserted through the side of the patty into the center. Remove the patties from heat when they reach 130°F / 54°C. They will carry over to 133 to 135°F / 56 to 57°C while resting. This is medium rare. It is the only correct doneness for this burger.

20. Place a slice of cheese on each patty immediately after pulling from the heat. Tent loosely with foil and rest for 3 to 4 minutes. Do not skip the rest — cutting into or biting a patty immediately will cause all the accumulated juices to run out.

21. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice each brioche bun and place cut-side down in the residual fat in the skillet over medium heat. Toast for 60 to 90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Watch carefully — brioche burns quickly due to its sugar content.
22. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous layer of smoky chipotle mayo on both the top and bottom bun cut surfaces. On the bottom bun, place a leaf of butter lettuce followed by 2 slices of tomato.
23. Place the cheesy patty on top of the tomato. Pile a generous spoonful of caramelized onions over the patty.
24. Lay 3 to 4 roasted yam rounds over the caramelized onions, slightly overlapping. The yams should be warm and fragrant — reheat briefly in the oven if needed.

25. Finish with a small pinch of flaky sea salt over the yams, then cap with the top bun. Press gently to compress slightly. Serve immediately alongside any remaining roasted yams. The burger waits for no one.
